pl-l2d25c8-d1e108.summary: States that freedom is threefold: from necessity, from sin, and from misery.
claims: There are three freedoms.

pl-l2d25c8-d1e111.summary: Explains freedom from necessity: choice is equally free from necessity before and after sin; it could not be coerced then nor now, so the will is judged before God, always free from necessity. Where necessity is, there is no freedom; without freedom, no will and so no merit. This freedom is in all, good and bad.
claims: The will is always free from necessity.
Without freedom from necessity there is no merit.

pl-l2d25c8-d1e116.summary: Introduces freedom from sin: 'where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom' (2 Cor 3:17); 'if the Son frees you, you will be free indeed' (John 8:36).
claims: Freedom from sin comes from the Spirit and the Son.

pl-l2d25c8-d1e123.summary: States that this freedom frees from slavery to sin and makes servants of justice, as slavery to sin makes one free from justice.
claims: Freedom from sin makes servants of justice.

pl-l2d25c8-d1e126.summary: Cites Rom 6:18, 20: freed from sin, you became servants of justice; when servants of sin, you were free from justice.
claims: One is either servant of sin or of justice.

pl-l2d25c8-d1e132.summary: States that man lost this freedom by sinning, so Augustine says he lost himself and free choice: lost was freedom from sin, not from necessity.
claims: Sin lost freedom from sin, not from necessity.

pl-l2d25c8-d1e135.summary: States that only those freed and restored by the Son through grace now have freedom from sin, not wholly without sin in this flesh but so that sin does not reign; this is true freedom producing good servitude to justice.
claims: Freedom from sin is restored by grace.
In this life sin remains but does not reign.

pl-l2d25c8-d1e141.summary: Cites the Enchiridion: no one is free to do justice unless freed from sin and become a servant of justice; this is true freedom for the joy of right action and pious servitude for obedience to the command.
claims: True freedom is servitude to justice.

pl-l2d25c8-d1e147.summary: Describes another, false freedom joined to bad servitude, the freedom for evil, where reason dissents from the will judging the deed should not be done; in doing good, reason agrees with will, and there is true and pious freedom.
claims: Freedom for evil is false freedom.

pl-l2d25c8-d1e151.summary: Cites the Enchiridion: what freedom can the enslaved have except when he delights to sin? He serves freely who gladly does his master's will; so the servant of sin is free to sin.
claims: The servant of sin is free only for sin.

pl-l2d25c8-d1e157.summary: Asks whether this freedom for evil is freedom of choice; if so, it is good, since freedom of choice is a natural good.

pl-l2d25c8-d1e162.summary: Reports some who think it is freedom of choice itself, always good, but more prone to evil because of sin's servitude, and so not called true freedom.
claims: One view: freedom for evil is free choice made prone to evil.

pl-l2d25c8-d1e165.summary: Reports others who think it is not freedom of choice but a proneness and crookedness for sinning, which comes from sin and is evil.
claims: Another view: freedom for evil is a sinful proneness.

pl-l2d25c8-d1e168.summary: Asks similarly whether the true freedom for doing justice is freedom of choice itself.

pl-l2d25c8-d1e171.summary: Reports some who say it is the same freedom, restored by grace, free for good with grace's help, not free for good without it.
claims: One view: freedom for good is free choice restored by grace.

pl-l2d25c8-d1e175.summary: Cites the Enchiridion: whence will freedom to do good come to one bound and sold unless the Son redeems him? Before that, how can anyone boast of free choice? So free choice is freed by grace to do good, and they say this true freedom is free choice freed and helped by God's grace.
claims: Free choice must be freed by grace to do good.

pl-l2d25c8-d1e178.summary: Reports others who think it is not free choice but another freedom, begun in the mind from grace and free choice when God restores it.
claims: Another view: freedom for good is a distinct freedom.

pl-l2d25c8-d1e181.summary: Gives Lombard's view: both the freedom for evil and the freedom for good are freedom of choice itself, named differently by cause: before grace it is free for evil; restored by grace it becomes free for good. The will is always free in some way, but not always good; it is good only when freed from sin, yet always free from necessity.
claims: Freedom for evil and for good are the same free choice.
The will is always free from necessity but good only when freed from sin.

pl-l2d25c8-d1e186.summary: Cites Augustine, De gratia et libero arbitrio: our will is always free but not always good; it is free from justice when serving sin, and then evil, or free from sin when serving justice, and then good.
claims: The will is always free but not always good.

pl-l2d25c8-d1e189.summary: Introduces freedom from misery: creation will be freed from the servitude of corruption into the freedom of the glory of God's children (Rom 8:21).
claims: Freedom from misery is eschatological.

pl-l2d25c8-d1e192.summary: States that man had this freedom before sin, lacking all misery, and will have it more fully in future beatitude; in this life between the first sin and final confirmation no one is free from misery. Hence free choice was diminished: before sin there was no difficulty or hindrance from the law of the members toward good, nor impulse toward evil.
claims: Freedom from misery existed before sin and will exist in glory.
No one in this life is free from misery.

pl-l2d25c8-d1e196.summary: States that now, by the law of the flesh, man is hindered from good and incited to evil, unable to will and accomplish good unless freed and helped by grace, since sin dwells in the flesh. Free choice, though always free, is not equally free in the good and the bad, nor for good and evil: freer in the good, where liberated, and freer for evil, which it can do by itself, than for good, which it cannot without grace.
claims: Fallen free choice is freer for evil than for good.
Good requires grace to free and help the will.

pl-l2d25c8.summary: Distinguishes three freedoms: from necessity, from sin, and from misery. Freedom from necessity belongs to the will equally before and after sin, in good and bad alike; where necessity is, there is no freedom, will, or merit. Freedom from sin (2 Cor 3:17; John 8:36) makes us servants of justice and was lost by sin; only those freed by grace have it, not wholly without sin but sin not reigning; this is true freedom with good servitude. There is also a false freedom for evil joined to bad servitude. Is the freedom for evil free choice itself? Some say yes, more prone to evil through sin; others that it is a proneness from sin. Is the true freedom for good free choice? Some say it is free choice restored by grace; others another freedom. Lombard holds both are free choice, named differently by cause: free for evil before grace, free for good after it; the will is always free but not always good (Augustine). Freedom from misery Adam had and the blessed will have fully; in this life no one has it. So free choice was diminished: once unhindered, now hindered by the law of the flesh, freer for evil, which it can do by itself, than for good, which needs grace.
claims: There are three freedoms: from necessity, from sin, and from misery.
Freedom from necessity is natural and is never lost; without it there is no merit.
Freedom from sin was lost by sin and is restored by grace.
Freedom for evil and freedom for good are the same free choice, named by different causes.
The will is always free, but not always good.
Freedom from misery belonged to Adam and will belong to the blessed, not to this life.
Fallen free choice is freer toward evil than toward good, which needs grace.
